questions.q: How does a driver’s field of view change at high speed?
options: It narrows, and the driver tends to focus far ahead and lose sensitivity to the sides
It widens and lets you see more at the sides
It stays exactly the same at every speed
It becomes sharper at the sides and blurred in the centre
questions.explain: At high speed the central field of view narrows, so it’s important to actively scan the road and not focus only straight ahead.

questions.q: What is hazard perception?
options: Seeing only warning signs on the road
Spotting early a situation that may develop into a hazard, not only a hazard that already exists
A skill only police officers need
Driving slowly enough to see everything
questions.explain: An experienced driver spots signs that warn of danger - like a ball rolling into the road - before the hazard itself appears.

questions.q: A driver is having a complex work call on a hands-free device, eyes on the road. He doesn’t notice a pedestrian who crossed, even though he was looking that way. What is the correct explanation?
options: This can’t happen if the hands are on the wheel
This only happens to inexperienced drivers
It’s a fault in the driver’s eyes, not his attention
Inattentional blindness - the brain, not just the eye, has to process what is seen, and a complex conversation takes up attention
questions.explain: Inattentional blindness makes you miss something obvious even when your gaze is pointed at it, because the brain - not just the eye - has to process the information.

questions.q: Which of the following is a good example of early “hazard perception”, before the hazard itself actually happened?
options: An advertising billboard at the side of the road
A ball rolling into the road near children playing
A tree a long way from the road
A parked car in an empty car park
questions.explain: A rolling ball warns of the chance that a child will run after it into the road - a driver with good hazard perception will slow down and prepare for it in advance.

questions.q: What are the early warning signs of fatigue while driving?
options: Increased sweating alone
Improved concentration and reaction time
Heavy eyes, repeated yawning and a slight drift within the lane
Increased appetite and thirst
questions.explain: Heavy eyes, yawning, trouble focusing your gaze and a slight drift within the lane are signs that must make a driver stop.

questions.q: What is microsleep?
options: A planned nap at the roadside
A general feeling of tiredness throughout the drive
Falling asleep for just a few seconds, sometimes with eyes open, without the driver noticing
Deep sleep of at least an hour
questions.explain: Microsleep lasts just a few seconds, and most drivers who experienced it don’t remember falling asleep at all.

questions.q: A driver feels very tired on a long night drive. What is the correct action?
options: Speed up to finish the drive faster
Stop somewhere safe and sleep, even briefly
Drink strong coffee and keep going without stopping
Open a window and turn up the music until arriving
questions.explain: The only solution to real fatigue is sleep; music, an open window and caffeine only delay the critical moment.

questions.q: During which hours is the risk of fatigue while driving highest?
options: Only on weekends
During the body’s natural low points - the small hours of the morning and the early afternoon
The risk is the same at every hour
Only between 12:00 and 14:00
questions.explain: In the small hours and mid-afternoon the body is at a natural low in alertness, and combined with accumulated lack of sleep, the risk is especially high.

questions.q: What is a driver allowed to do with a mobile phone while the vehicle is moving?
options: Read a text message when the car is moving slowly in traffic
Hold it and talk without a hands-free device
Take photos holding the phone while driving
Use it only through a hands-free device, without holding it
questions.explain: Regulation 28(b) forbids holding or using a phone without a hands-free device, and forbids sending or reading a text message - {{fine:phone-handheld}} and {{points:phone-handheld}} points.

questions.q: What is the difference between manual, visual and cognitive distraction?
options: Cognitive is only when talking on the phone without a hands-free device
Visual is only driving at night
There’s no difference, they’re all the same thing
Manual - hands off the wheel; visual - eyes off the road; cognitive - the mind busy with something else even if the eyes and hands are fine
questions.explain: A combination of all three types of distraction at once, like writing a text message, is the most dangerous.

questions.q: A driver travels at {{fact:speed.urban}} in the city and glances sideways for about 2 seconds. About how many metres does he cover without looking at the road?
options: About 28 metres
About 14 metres
About 50 metres
About 5 metres
questions.explain: At {{fact:speed.urban}} the car covers about 14 metres per second; in 2 seconds of glancing sideways, it covers about 28 metres without seeing the road.

questions.q: Why can even a hands-free conversation distract a driver, even though it is legal and their hands are on the wheel?
options: A complex conversation takes up cognitive attention, even without manual or visual distraction
It is only forbidden in heavy vehicles
A hands-free device damages hearing
It doesn’t distract at all, that’s why it’s legal
questions.explain: The brain has limited attention; a conversation that requires thinking - arguing, planning, remembering - takes attention away from the road even without holding a phone.

questions.q: What does regulation 28A of the Traffic Regulations forbid?
options: Operating a display visible from the driver’s seat while driving, that is not a control or navigation display
Wearing sunglasses
Operating a navigation display while driving
Holding a printed map in the car
questions.explain: Regulation 28A forbids a display visible from the driver’s seat while driving, except a vehicle control or navigation display.

questions.q: What is the maximum alcohol concentration allowed in a breath test for a regular driver (not a new driver, under 24, or driving a heavy or public vehicle)?
options: 100 micrograms per litre of exhaled breath
{{fact:alcohol.strict.breath}}
{{fact:alcohol.general.breath}}
500 micrograms per litre of exhaled breath
questions.explain: The threshold for a regular driver is {{fact:alcohol.general.breath}}; the stricter threshold, {{fact:alcohol.strict.breath}}, applies to certain groups of drivers.

questions.q: Who does the strict alcohol threshold of {{fact:alcohol.strict.breath}} in breath apply to?
options: Only bus drivers
Only drivers over 60
All drivers, with no exceptions
A new driver, a driver under {{fact:alcohol.strict.age}}, a driver of a commercial or work vehicle over {{fact:alcohol.strict.weight_threshold}}, and a driver of a public vehicle
questions.explain: Traffic Ordinance, section 64B, sets a strict threshold, close to zero, for these groups.

questions.q: When is it permitted to drink an intoxicating beverage in any amount and drive immediately afterwards?
options: Only when travelling a short distance
Never - impairment to driving ability begins from the first sip
When there’s another passenger in the car who can “keep watch”
After a large meal
questions.explain: The legal threshold is an enforcement limit, not an assurance: impairment to reaction time and judgement begins even before the threshold.

questions.q: What is the “presumption” the law establishes regarding an alcohol concentration measured in a test?
options: That the measured concentration was also in the driver’s body during the {{fact:alcohol.presumption_hours}} hours before the test, unless proven otherwise
That the concentration is valid for a week ahead
That the concentration drops immediately after the test
That the concentration was measured by mistake
questions.explain: Section 64B of the Ordinance sets a presumption that the measured concentration was also in the driver’s body during the hours before the test.

questions.q: A driver was required by a police officer to take a breath test, and refused. What is correct?
options: There’s no consequence at all, you can simply refuse and keep driving
You may refuse only once a year
The refusal itself is a serious offence, carrying the same penalty as drunkenness
The refusal only results in a verbal warning
questions.explain: Refusing to be tested is a separate, serious offence, {{points:refuse-sobriety-test}} points - “saving yourself” by refusing doesn’t help.

questions.q: One evening, a person drank a large amount of alcohol. The next morning he feels “fine” and plans to drive. What is correct?
options: Strong coffee in the morning neutralises the remaining alcohol
Once he’s slept a bit, the alcohol has certainly left his body
The liver breaks down alcohol slowly and steadily - his alcohol concentration may still be above the legal threshold, even if he feels subjectively fine
It only depends on body weight, not on the time that has passed
questions.explain: Breaking down alcohol in the liver is a relatively slow, steady process that cannot be sped up; heavy drinking in the evening can leave a concentration above the threshold even in the morning.

questions.q: A driver is taking a prescription medicine whose leaflet says “may cause drowsiness and impair driving alertness”. What should he do?
options: Drive only on slow urban roads
Take the warning seriously, and when in doubt consult a pharmacist or doctor before driving
Take a lower dose than prescribed and drive as usual
Ignore it, because the medicine is legal and prescribed
questions.explain: A leaflet’s warning about driving was written exactly for this situation; when in doubt, ask a pharmacist or doctor before driving.

questions.q: By law, when is a driver considered “drunk” because of drugs?
options: The law doesn’t address drugs, only alcohol
Only if caught using a drug inside the vehicle itself
Only if he admitted to using a drug
When a dangerous drug or its breakdown products are in his body, or when he is under its influence
questions.explain: Traffic Ordinance, section 64B(a), equates a dangerous drug with alcohol: both make a driver “drunk” for legal purposes.

questions.q: Which common types of medicine can impair alertness while driving?
options: Vitamins and mineral supplements
Skin ointments
Sleeping pills, sedatives and older antihistamines for allergies
Moisturising eye drops alone
questions.explain: Sleeping pills, sedatives and older-generation antihistamines are known to cause drowsiness and impair alertness.

questions.q: What is the effect of anger and stress on driving?
options: They improve reaction time
They narrow attention and increase the tendency to take risks, similar to fatigue
They have no effect on safe driving
They only affect older drivers
questions.explain: Anger and stress impair judgement and patience and increase the tendency to take risks - exactly like fatigue.

questions.q: Another driver behaves rudely toward you on the road - prolonged honking and dangerous tailgating. What is the correct behaviour?
options: Honk back and slow down to “teach them a lesson”
Stop in the middle of the road and get out to talk to them
Increase your distance, don’t confront them, and if needed drive to a public place and call the police
Speed up to “beat” them on the road
questions.explain: Confronting an aggressive driver escalates the risk; the safe way is to pull away and not react.

questions.q: Why are young and new drivers at higher risk, beyond inexperience alone?
options: They always drive too slowly
The law places no restrictions on them at all
Their confidence in their own driving ability is usually higher than their actual ability
They always drive with an accompanying driver
questions.explain: A combination of overconfidence, excitement and peer pressure increases risk-taking among young drivers.
